paragraphs.source_en:
Pref. Count Maddalo] To some extent, a portrait of Lord Byron. S. remarked to Leigh Hunt of the
poem, ‘two of the characters you will recognize’ (L ii 108), presumably Byron and S. himself as Maddalo
and Julian. Byron was living at the Palazzo Mocenigo in Venice when S. visited. Cp. Thomas Medwin,
Conversations of Lord Byron, ed. Ernest J. Lovell (Princeton, 1966), 119: ‘S., I remember, draws a very
beautiful picture of the tranquil pleasures of Venice in a poem which he has not yet published, and in
which he does not make me cut a good figure. It describes an evening we passed together.’ The name is
used for a courtier in S.’s drafted scene for a drama on the life of Tasso (see Longman ii 365–9) and may
be connected to the French matelot (seaman); S. often referred to Byron as Albe and to Allegra as Alba;
pseudonyms and nicknames were often used (privately and publicly) by the S. circle.
